Body: Suggestion: this replacement handles layered config loads, but the update and updateGlobal write paths later in this file still use raw mergeDeep. If an existing config has tool_output.max_lines or tool_output.max_bytes and the API writes { tool_output: { truncate: false } }, the persisted JSON can keep the old thresholds beside truncate: false, which this schema now rejects on the next load. Consider applying the same replacement semantics in those write paths when either side changes tool_output mode.

Out of curiosity, I was looking at some of the other plugins (like `github-copilot`, etc.) and noticed they also make custom `fetch` calls during their specific OAuth or authentication flows.

Since these custom authentication fetches aren't wrapped by the new main provider timeout, are they still vulnerable to infinite socket hangs if their respective APIs stall during login? Should we consider abstracting this `timeoutController` logic so it can be easily applied to all custom provider token/auth fetches?
`C:\` cannot use FFF here: FFF rejects filesystem roots, so worst-case broad searches immediately fall back to ripgrep.
`**/opencode.json{,c}` fell back to ripgrep while `**/opencode.json` used FFF. Common glob syntax appears to miss the new path.
Shouldn't a successful FFF search with no matches return `[]`? `**/opencode.jsonc` under `~` fell back to ripgrep and then failed on an inaccessible directory.

The TUI `@` picker does not hit this branch: it calls `find.files({ query, workspace })`, which resolves to `kind === "all"`. I verified this headlessly against the PR checkout. On Windows, even an explicit `type: "file"` call still returned `mode=cache` because FFF results use `/` while the cached paths use `\`.

Suggestion: when `tool_output` is false, this condition prevents writing to disk, but `full += chunk` still runs on every chunk even though `full` is never read in the disabled path (the final output comes from `list`/`raw`). For large outputs this keeps a second copy of the whole stream in memory. Consider skipping the `full` buffer entirely when `limits` is `None` so disabled truncation only stores the one buffer needed to return the untruncated output.

The `Promise.resolve().then(...).catch(() => {})` wrapper is an unusual pattern for swallowing errors from `Bus.publish`. A direct `try { await Bus.publish(...) } catch {}` would be clearer and equivalent. Also consider logging the swallowed publish error at debug level rather than silently discarding it, to aid future troubleshooting when events are unexpectedly missing.

Replacing `ConfigParse.schema(Info, config, item)` with a raw `Schema.decodeUnknownExit` likely loses the detailed, formatted validation error that `ConfigParse.schema` produced (it typically formats `parsed.cause` into a human-readable message including the failing field and reason). The user-facing message here is now just `"Failed to parse agent <path>"`, which is significantly less actionable than what `loadMode` and the previous `load` produced. Consider formatting `parsed.cause` into the reported message (e.g. via `ArrayFormatter` or the same helper `ConfigParse.schema` uses) so users can tell *why* their agent file is invalid.

These tests rely on fixed `Bun.sleep(10)` delays to synchronize with asynchronous Bus event delivery, which is flaky on slow CI machines. Prefer awaiting a deterministic signal — e.g. collecting events through a promise that resolves on first matching event with a generous timeout, or subscribing before `load()` and awaiting `load()`'s completion without additional sleeps if `Bus.publish` is awaited inside `report`. Note also that the pre-`load()` `sleep(10)` serves no apparent purpose since no async work has been triggered yet.

The dynamic `import("@/session/session")` is performed on every failure inside `report`. Since this helper is module-local and called from the same file, consider hoisting the dynamic import to module scope (cached promise) or moving it out of the hot path. This was likely originally inlined to avoid a circular import; if so, a brief comment explaining the rationale would help future maintainers, and caching the resolved module avoids repeated module-resolution work on bursts of invalid files.

These assertions are Windows-specific (they rely on Windows casing/"\\" handling) but the test currently runs on all platforms via `it.instance`. On non-Windows runners this will fail because path normalization is intentionally disabled when `process.platform !== "win32"`. Add a platform guard (or skip) so the test suite remains portable.

This assertion is Windows-specific (case-insensitive matching + backslash normalization). Since `PathIdentity` only applies that behavior on `win32`, this test will fail on non-Windows CI runners unless it is guarded or skipped.

`toStoragePath()` performs synchronous `realpathSync.native()` calls on Windows. Because helpers like `absoluteEquals()` and `relativePath()` call into `toStoragePath()`, this can put synchronous filesystem I/O on hot paths (e.g., request-time query construction) and repeatedly re-stat the same directory. Consider memoizing `realWindowsPath()` results to avoid repeated sync I/O for identical inputs.

`PathStorage.relative(input.path)` is computed twice here, which repeats validation/normalization work and makes it harder to keep the `eq` and `like` branches consistent. Consider computing it once and reusing the value.

This sentence is clearer than before, but it now implies both actions always happen (look in current directory AND traverse). If the intent is 'look in current directory; if not found, traverse upward', consider wording that preserves that conditional behavior (e.g., '...in the current directory, then traverses up...').
This mutates state during layout; could it desync scroll until resize?

`Bus.subscribe(...)` isn’t unsubscribed, so these tests can leak listeners across test cases (leading to cross-test interference and flakiness as more subscriptions accumulate). Return an unsubscribe/dispose handle from `subscribeErrors` (if `Bus.subscribe` provides one) and ensure it’s called (e.g., in `afterEach` or `try/finally` around `await wait`).

The timeout path resolves successfully (rather than rejecting), which makes failures less explicit and can be harder to diagnose (you only fail later via assertions). Consider making the timeout reject with a clear error (including `pattern` and collected `errors`) and/or increasing the default `timeoutMs` to reduce CI flakiness.

The user-facing published message for schema decode failures is always the generic `Failed to parse agent ...`, which loses the actionable validation details (e.g., which field/type failed). Consider including a short formatted summary from `parsed.cause` (or the schema errors) in `message` so users can fix the invalid frontmatter without digging into logs.

The `write` endpoint schema doesn’t include the workspace/directory routing query fields, but the generated SDK method builds `directory`/`workspace` query params and the rest of the File API endpoints include `WorkspaceRoutingQueryFields`. If your HttpApi layer validates requests, this mismatch can cause PUT requests to be rejected (unexpected query params) or routed with missing context. Recommended fix: define a `FileWriteQuery` that includes `...WorkspaceRoutingQueryFields` and attach it to the endpoint as `query`, and update the handler signature accordingly to consume `ctx.query`.

The SDK exposes `directory`/`workspace` on `file.write()` and will serialize them as query params, but the server endpoint definition for `write` currently has no query schema. Either (preferred) add the routing query schema to the server endpoint, or remove these parameters from the SDK generation for this endpoint to keep client/server contract consistent.

Worker selection doesn’t cover the language IDs you’re setting via `getLanguageForFile()`. In particular, `tsx` maps to `typescriptreact` and `jsx` maps to `javascriptreact`, which will currently fall through to the generic `editorWorker` and lose TS/JS language services. Also, if you start returning `sass` as a language id, it should be routed to the CSS worker too. Fix: extend the `label` checks to include `typescriptreact`/`javascriptreact` (and `sass` if used).

This sets `self.MonacoEnvironment` at module evaluation time. In SSR/non-browser contexts (or certain test runners), `self` may be undefined and importing this module would throw before `onMount` runs. Safer approach: guard the assignment (e.g., only set it when `typeof self !== \"undefined\"`), or perform the assignment inside `onMount`.

Two correctness issues in the language map: (1) `getLanguageForFile()` lowercases extensions, so the `R` key is unreachable and should be removed to avoid confusion. (2) Mapping `sass` to `scss` sets the wrong Monaco language id for `.sass` files (indent-based syntax is different). Fix: drop the `R` entry and map `sass` to `sass` (and ensure the Monaco worker routing handles `sass`).

Once `editing` is enabled, there’s no way to exit the overlay without saving (no cancel/close path). This can trap users if they open the editor accidentally or decide not to save. Consider adding a close/cancel button and/or ESC handling that calls `setEditing(false)` (optionally with a dirty-state confirmation if content changed).

Suggestion: consider only calling `touchPart` after this delta is actually applied. Right now a delta for a part that is not in local state still marks the part as live, then the hydration merge treats the HTTP snapshot as stale and drops it because there is no current part to preserve. Moving the revision touch below the `!parts` / `!result.found` guards would keep discarded deltas from deleting the hydrated part.

Appending `EOL` unconditionally can introduce double newlines (e.g., when `text`/`out` already ends with `\\n`), which changes CLI output and may break snapshot tests or parsers consuming stderr. Consider only appending a newline when the string does not already end with `\\n`/`EOL`, or preserve the previous behavior and ensure callers include the newline explicitly.

The provided `fetch` implementation only accepts `Request`, but `typeof fetch` is `(input: RequestInfo | URL, init?: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>`. The `as unknown as typeof fetch` cast can hide real incompatibilities if the SDK ever calls fetch with a URL/string + init. Prefer implementing a wrapper with the full fetch signature (constructing a `Request` from `input`/`init`) so it is actually compatible without unsafe casts.

This test mutates global state (`process.env` and `Flag.*`) but does not restore prior values, which can leak into other tests running in the same process. Consider capturing the previous env/flag values before setting them and restoring them in an `afterAll` (or restoring per-test in `afterEach`), so other suites aren’t affected by the embedded-auth configuration.

These calls pass `args.password`/`args.username` unconditionally into `ServerAuth.headers(...)`. If either argument can be `undefined`, this may produce incorrect/invalid auth headers (or force auth behavior unexpectedly) depending on `ServerAuth.headers` implementation. Prefer only setting `headers` when credentials are actually present (or ensure `ServerAuth.headers` returns `undefined`/`{}` when inputs are missing) to avoid sending malformed auth headers.

If `createOpencodeClient` ultimately forwards to fetch, consider typing this as `HeadersInit` (or the SDK’s expected header type) to avoid unnecessary conversions and allow broader caller compatibility.

These tests write to `Global.Path.state/kv.json`, which can make the suite non-hermetic and potentially mutate a real user state directory depending on how `Global.Path.state` is configured in the test environment. Prefer isolating state per test (e.g., temp directory) and cleaning it up afterward, or using a test-specific override for `Global.Path.state` so the suite can safely run on developer machines and in parallel.

The fetch stub returns `undefined` for any unexpected request, which can lead to opaque failures (or timeouts in `wait(...)`) if the component makes an additional call or the request path changes. Consider making the default branch explicit (e.g., throw with the unexpected URL/path, or return a failing JSON) so the test fails fast with a clear cause.

`tabForSession()` normalizes subagent routes to their root session by rewriting `sessionId`/`href` to the root session. Any code that identifies the “current tab” via `makeSessionHref(params.dir, params.id)` (i.e., using the routed child id) will no longer match an existing tab when the route points at a child session. In particular, `removeSessions` still derives `currentHref` from `params.id`, which can prevent detecting/removing the active tab and leave tab navigation/close commands in a broken state when a root session is removed while viewing a child route.

Fixed in d99e29306b. Subagent routes still never create tabs: tabForSession normalizes them to the root tab. removeDeletedSessionTabs now handles the deletion-only case where the routed child and its normalized root tab are both removed, and navigates to the next surviving tab. Added a regression test for that scenario.

When `hydrateSessionLineage` loads an ancestor that is already archived, the code returns early without recording that ancestor as unavailable. That means subsequent syncs can repeatedly re-fetch the same archived ancestor because `available()` only consults `store.session_unavailable`. Consider marking archived ancestors as unavailable to prevent repeated network requests and to keep availability state consistent.

Only the root session's caches are dropped when an archive event marks an entire cached subtree unavailable. This leaves message/todo/status caches for descendant sessions in memory even though they are now unavailable. Dropping caches for the full `sessionIDs` set avoids stale data and reduces memory usage.

Only the deleted session's caches are dropped, even though the handler marks the entire cached subtree unavailable via `sessionIDs`. This can retain caches (messages, todos, status, etc.) for descendant sessions that are now effectively deleted/unavailable. Drop caches for all `sessionIDs` to keep the store consistent and free memory.

In the non-archived `session.updated` path, the handler always clears `session_unavailable[info.id]`. If a session was previously marked unavailable (e.g., a descendant marked unavailable when its root was archived/deleted), a later non-archived update would clear that flag and allow the session to be treated as available again. Unless the backend explicitly supports "restore/unarchive" semantics, it’s safer to ignore non-archived updates for sessions already marked unavailable.

`Persist.serverGlobal` builds remote keys using `server:${scope}:${key}`. Because `scope` values often include ":" (e.g. `https://...`), this format can produce ambiguous/colliding keys if any persisted `key` ever contains `:` (e.g. scope="a:b", key="c" vs scope="a", key="b:c"). Consider using the existing null-byte scoped-key encoding (`ScopedKey.from(...)`) to guarantee unique, parse-safe server partitioning.

`createHomeSessionStatus` uses `activeServer` to gate unseen/error/permission indicators, but `isWorking` and `tint` still read from `sessionStore` even when `activeServer()` is false. This can cause the status indicator to show (spinner/tint) for non-active servers, which contradicts the `activeServer` gating and can lead to inconsistent UI.

`loadedSessionTreeIDs` currently scans the full `sessions` list for every queued node (nested loops). That makes it O(n²) in the size of the loaded session list and can become noticeably expensive when called frequently (e.g. on archive/delete paths). Building a parent→children index once keeps traversal O(n).

This archived filter treats `archived: 0` as not archived because it uses a falsy check. Elsewhere in this PR archive handling was updated to treat `0` as archived (i.e. `archived !== undefined`). Use an explicit undefined check here too so navigation/next-session selection is consistent.

This test name is misleading: the expectations show the whole tree is marked unavailable (`root`, `child`, and `other`), not only the archived root. Renaming the test will make the intent of the behavior clearer and prevent future confusion when reading failures.

`tabsEnriched().map((resolve) => resolve())` allocates a new array and new tab objects on every reactive update, which can cause unnecessary re-renders and defeats the memoization benefits of `mapArray`. Iterating the `mapArray` result directly keeps per-tab computations stable and reduces churn.
Fixed in 4a2f096445. Persist.serverGlobal now uses ScopedKey.from(scope, key), with a regression covering colon-containing scope/key pairs.
Fixed in 4a2f096445. Inactive-server status projection now evaluates lazily and returns no working/tint state without reading the inactive session store; regression added.

The SQL migration adds a new `NOT NULL` column without a `DEFAULT`. In SQLite, `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL` will fail if `session_message` already contains rows unless a default is provided. The TS migration uses `DEFAULT 0`; the SQL artifact should match (e.g., add `DEFAULT 0`) to avoid failing migrations in production.

The fallback backfill uses a correlated `COUNT(*)` per row, which is O(n²) over `session_message` and can become very slow on large datasets. SQLite supports window functions; using something like `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY session_id ORDER BY time_created, id) - 1` (and then `COALESCE(event.seq, computed_seq)`) would compute the ordering in a single pass and be much more scalable.

This insert-select hardcodes the `project_directory` table/column names as raw SQL while the rest of the file uses Drizzle table objects (e.g., `ProjectDirectoryTable` for deletes). That makes schema refactors easier to miss and reduces type safety. Prefer using Drizzle's insert/select APIs if supported for your dialect, or at least use the table object's declared name/columns (e.g., via identifiers) so schema changes don't silently break this query.

`createContext<LocalImageResolver>()` is typed as always providing a resolver, but at runtime the default context value is `undefined` when no provider is mounted. This can lead to unsound typing (callers may treat the resolver as always defined). Make the context type explicitly optional (e.g., `LocalImageResolver | undefined`) and/or pass an explicit default value so the hook’s return type matches reality.

The generated HTML interpolates `href`, `text` (alt), and `title` directly into attribute values without escaping. If any contain quotes or angle brackets, this can break markup and potentially create injection opportunities before sanitization runs. Escape/encode these attribute values (at least `"`/`&`/`<`/`>`) before concatenation, and consider URL-encoding `href` where appropriate.

Falling back to `src=""` when `href` is missing can trigger an unintended request to the current document URL in some browsers and produce noisy network traffic. Prefer omitting the `src` attribute entirely, returning an empty string (don’t render an image), or using a harmless placeholder like `src="data:,"`.

These async resolver calls are not canceled/guarded across re-renders or unmounts. A promise may resolve after the element is replaced by `morphdom` or after cleanup, causing updates to detached/stale DOM nodes. Add a disposal/epoch guard inside the effect (e.g., incrementing token or `let disposed=false` with `onCleanup`) and check it (and optionally `img.isConnected`) before assigning `img.src`.

During streaming updates, `morphdom` may replace `` elements, which can cause repeated `resolver()` calls for the same path while previous requests are still in flight (since the new element won’t have `img.src` yet). Consider deduplicating by caching in-flight/resolved lookups keyed by `directory + path`, or marking elements as “loading/resolved” via a data attribute to prevent redundant reads.

`rawPath` comes from untrusted Markdown and is passed directly to `client.file.read({ path: rawPath })`. This enables path traversal attempts (e.g., `../`, absolute paths, or platform-specific prefixes) unless the server strictly enforces sandboxing. Add client-side validation/normalization (reject `..`, absolute paths, and protocol-like strings) and ensure the server endpoint guarantees reads are constrained to the intended directory scope.

Swallowing all resolver errors makes failures silent and hard to debug (e.g., missing files, permissions, server issues). Consider at least logging in non-production builds or capturing the error in a debug channel/telemetry, while still returning `undefined` to keep the UI resilient.

`createMemo(() => { …ensureServerCtx… })` is used for side effects but its value is never read. In Solid, `createMemo` is lazy, so this block may never execute and server contexts may not be created when the server list changes. Use `createEffect` for eager side effects tied to reactivity.

`scope` is captured as a plain value (`const scope = server.scope()`) and then used to key terminal caches/persistence. This makes terminal state stick to whatever server was active at provider init, so switching active servers can leak/incorrectly reuse terminal tabs across servers and bypass the intended server scoping.

`instructions` is arbitrary plugin-provided text; the contract does not define `:` as a code discriminator. This now drops useful no-colon instructions entirely. For example, bundled DigitalOcean returns no-colon instructions explaining its token/router behavior and that users should rerun `/connect`, but this view replaces them with the generic browser message. Please preserve non-code instructions as body text, and use an explicit signal if the UI needs to distinguish a confirmation code.

This should force a fresh probe when entering the WSL OpenCode step or when the selected distro changes. Otherwise `opencodeChecks[distro]` can remain stale if the user upgrades/downgrades OpenCode inside WSL outside the desktop app.

Because this cache never goes stale, version-sensitive WSL state needs explicit invalidation or forced reprobe. Otherwise external WSL changes, like downgrading `opencode`, can continue showing the previous version.

When removing a WSL server, also clear cached per-distro probe state like `opencodeChecks[distro]` and `distroProbes[distro]`. Otherwise remove/re-add can reuse stale version data for the same distro.

This fallback should use `allServers()` instead of `store.list` because WSL and local sidecar servers come from `props.servers`, not the persisted HTTP server list. Otherwise removing the active server can ignore valid sidecar entries or select the wrong fallback.

Thanks, addressed in `46399ef`. I removed the character heuristic entirely (`asciiChars` / `nonAsciiChars` are gone). The live footer now counts committed assistant/reasoning stream chunks as a provider-neutral fallback and keeps the `~` marker because this is still not provider/billing usage. Provider-reported usage/cost remains authoritative and replaces the fallback when it arrives.

The `chars` cleanup is no longer applicable after that change because the char-count fields were removed.

`findContextLimit` treats `v.limit.context = 0` as falsy and incorrectly falls back to the base model context limit. If `0` is a meaningful value in this system (it is treated specially elsewhere), this will return the wrong limit. Use an undefined/null check instead (e.g., check `v?.limit?.context !== undefined`) so `0` is preserved.

`usable()` correctly resolves a variant-aware `limit`, but still computes `maxOutputTokens` using `input.model` (which likely reflects the *base* model limits). If a variant overrides output limits, the reserved/output calculation can be wrong, which can make overflow detection too aggressive or too lax for that variant. Consider computing max output tokens using the effective limit (e.g., pass a model object whose `limit` is `effectiveLimit(...)`, or extend `ProviderTransform.maxOutputTokens` to accept a limit override/variant).

The `||` fallback will treat a valid context limit of `0` as falsy and fall back to `model?.limit.context`, which can display an incorrect percent. Prefer nullish coalescing so `0` is preserved (e.g., compute the variant context limit and then `??` fall back to the base context limit). This same pattern appears in other UI call sites added in this PR.

Variant context-limit lookup logic (and the local `VariantConfig` typing) is duplicated across multiple TUI components (and similarly in the app metrics). Consider extracting a shared helper (e.g., `getContextLimit(model, variant)`), or reusing existing shared logic (`effectiveLimit`/`findContextLimit` equivalents on the frontend) to keep behavior consistent and reduce the chance of future drift.
